definition: In linguistics, realization is the process by which some kind of surface representation is derived from its underlying representation; that is, the way in which some abstract object of linguistic analysis comes to be produced in actual language.
details: Phonemes are often said to be realized by speech sounds. The different sounds that can realize a particular phoneme are called its allophones. Realization is also a subtask of natural language generation, which involves creating an actual text in a human language (English, French, etc.) from a syntactic representation. There are a number of software packages available for realization, most of which have been developed by academic research groups in NLG. The remainder of this article concerns realization of this kind.

explainer.lead: Realization is how an abstract linguistic representation becomes an actual surface form. It matters in speech and text generation, where abstract units must be turned into concrete output.

tiers.eli5: Like a recipe (the abstract plan) being turned into an actual baked cake (the real output).
tiers.practitioner: In natural language generation, engineers realize a syntactic representation into actual text, often with academic software packages. Pitfall: realization is a distinct subtask, so treating it as identical to planning conflates two stages.
tiers.paperLevel: The process by which a surface representation is derived from its underlying representation; phonemes are realized by speech sounds, and the variant sounds realizing one phoneme are its allophones. In NLG it is the subtask producing human-language text from a syntactic representation.

explainer.example: A phoneme is realized as different speech sounds (allophones) depending on context; in NLG, a syntactic structure is turned into an English sentence.
